bull.b: The licensing and marketing framework creates a defined route to commercialize Loop’s technology without requiring the company to operate every facility itself. Royalty and sales-linked fees could support recurring participation in future production, while partner incentives are tied to net sales and facility scale.

A process aimed at hard-to-recycle PET addresses a persistent waste problem and supports demand from packaging and textile customers seeking recycled inputs. If the technology performs as intended at commercial scale, this differentiated feedstock capability could strengthen Loop’s position in circular materials.

Separating the chairman and CEO roles and creating a board-led committee adds dedicated oversight during the transition from technology development to project execution. Its broad mandate can improve strategic discipline around financing, partnerships and commercialization of the intellectual-property platform.

bear.b: Extremely negative gross and net margins show that current operations do not cover the cost structure and that the business has not yet demonstrated sustainable operating leverage. Continued losses could consume capital, constrain investment in commercialization and make funding future projects more difficult.

bear.t: Negative equity and eroded capital base
bear.b: The shift from positive to negative equity indicates that accumulated losses have materially weakened the capital base. Although reported debt is modest, negative equity reduces financial flexibility, complicates leverage assessment and leaves fewer internal resources available to support project development or absorb setbacks.

Sustained operating and free-cash-flow deficits mean Loop is not currently funding itself through operations. Ongoing burn increases dependence on external financing and raises execution risk because the company must secure capital while also funding commercialization and its planned India joint venture.
